rows.answer: Photorealistic talking-head avatars create identity-security risks because an attacker can steal a user's avatar and replicate its appearance and voice, making it indistinguishable from the real person by sight or sound alone, thus enabling impersonation attacks and identity fraud [S1]. rows.question: How does the STMC method combine timeline-conditioned motion predictions?
expected_answer_points: It runs a pretrained diffusion model on each prompt independently at each denoising step, then stitches predictions in space and time.
rows.answer: The STMC method combines timeline-conditioned motion predictions by first partitioning the multi-track timeline into body-part timelines using LLM-based labeling to assign text prompts to specific body parts (e.g., arms, legs, torso) [S2]. It then independently denoises each text prompt's motion crop, extracting body-part motions from the denoised outputs [S1]. These body-part motions are spatially stitched together using the body-part annotations to form a composite motion [S2]. Temporal stitching ensures smooth transitions between overlapping prompts by aligning the motion crops across time intervals [S1]. The final composite motion is re-noised at each step and passed to the next denoising iteration [S1].

rows.question: How were natural-language training instructions created for InstructAvatar's emotional talking videos?

rows.question: Why does InstructAvatar gate its text conditioning with a zero-initialised convolution?
expected_answer_points: It starts from a pretrained emotion-unaware talking-head model; the zero convolution makes the text branch initially a no-op so instructions are injected gradually, stabilising training. Removing it badly hurts lip sync (SyncD 12.832).
rows.answer: InstructAvatar gates its text conditioning with a zero-initialised convolution to gradually inject text instructions into a pre-trained emotion-unaware model without disrupting the learned parameters. This mechanism ensures that at training initialization, the hidden states remain unchanged (hi = hi−1), corresponding to the no-instruction setting. The zero convolution acts as a gate, allowing text control to be introduced incrementally, thereby stabilizing training and preserving the abundant knowledge from previous models. This design enables effective fine-grained control over emotion and motion while maintaining the model's stability and performance [S1].

rows.question: How does Real3D-Portrait fill in the background area that the person covers in the source image?

rows.answer: Real3D-Portrait fills the background area occupied by the foreground (i.e., the person) in the source image using a K-nearest-neighbor (KNN)-based inpainting method. rows.question: Why does MDM-SMPL represent poses with SMPL joint rotations, and what speed-up does it bring?
expected_answer_points: Parent-relative SMPL rotations are easier to stitch by body part than root-relative joint positions and avoid test-time SMPL fitting; with 100 instead of 1000 diffusion steps it samples in under 5 s versus minutes for MDM.
rows.answer: MDM-SMPL represents poses with SMPL joint rotations to avoid expensive test-time optimization by using a body-part-stitchable, local kinematic representation that propagates changes through the body hierarchy, ensuring coherent motion across joints [S1]. This representation enables direct SMPL pose parameter output, eliminating the need for optimization-based fitting methods typically used in prior work [S3]. The model achieves a 10× speed-up in sampling by reducing the number of diffusion steps from 1000 to 100, combined with pre-computed text embeddings, resulting in average generation times under 5 seconds [S5].
